subject: Environment
description: Sea level rise, glacier retreat, ocean acidification, IPCC AR6, El Niño / La Niña

questions.stem: The MAJOR cause of recent sea-level rise globally is:

options.option_text: Increased rainfall on oceans
Thermal expansion of seawater + melting of land-based ice (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctic)
Earthquakes
Tide variations

questions.explanation: Two main drivers — (1) THERMAL EXPANSION (warmer water occupies more volume; ~40-50% historical contribution); (2) MELTING land-based ice (glaciers + Greenland + Antarctica; growing share post-1990). Sea ice melting (Arctic) does NOT raise sea level (already floating, displacing equivalent volume per Archimedes). Current rate ~3.6 mm/year, accelerating. Total since 1900: ~21-24 cm. IPCC AR6 SSP5-8.5 worst case: ~1.0 m by 2100. Bangladesh, Maldives, Sundarbans — most vulnerable.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: 'Ocean acidification' refers to the ocean becoming more:

options.option_text: Alkaline
Acidic — CO₂ dissolves in water → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; ocean pH dropping
Salty
Hot

questions.explanation: Atmospheric CO₂ → dissolves in oceans → forms carbonic acid → releases H⁺ → lowers pH. Pre-industrial pH ~8.2 → current ~8.05 (a 30% increase in [H⁺] since pH is logarithmic). Threatens calcifying organisms — coral, shellfish, plankton — whose shells dissolve in lower-pH water. 'Other CO₂ problem' alongside warming. Ocean has absorbed ~30% of human CO₂ emissions, slowing atmospheric warming but accelerating acidification. Saturation states (Ω) for aragonite + calcite track this.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) was established in 1988 by:

options.option_text: UN General Assembly directly
WMO (World Meteorological Organization) and UNEP
World Bank
UNESCO

questions.explanation: IPCC — established 1988 by WMO + UNEP. Headquartered in Geneva. Three working groups + Task Force on Greenhouse Gas Inventories. Produces Assessment Reports (AR1 1990, AR6 2021-23) summarising peer-reviewed climate science for policymakers. Doesn't conduct original research. Awarded Nobel Peace Prize 2007 (jointly with Al Gore). Current chair (2023-) — Jim Skea (UK). India represented by Ministry of Environment, IITM Pune.
questions.subject: Environment

options.option_text: Cold-water phase of ENSO
Warm-water phase of ENSO — abnormal warming of central + eastern equatorial Pacific that disrupts global weather
Indian monsoon system
Antarctic ice cycle

questions.explanation: ENSO (El Niño-Southern Oscillation) has two phases. EL NIÑO ('the boy child' — Spanish, named by Peruvian fishermen who first noted it around Christmas) — Pacific trade winds weaken; warm water sloshes east; severe rainfall in S America, drought in Indonesia, Australia, India (often deficient monsoon). LA NIÑA (girl child) — opposite, intensified trade winds, cool central Pacific, often strong Indian monsoon. Cycle every 2-7 years. Modulated by climate change (debated whether becoming more frequent / extreme).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 'Greenhouse Gas Protocol' classifies emissions into three scopes. Scope-3 emissions are:

options.option_text: Direct emissions from owned sources
All other indirect emissions across the value chain — supplier upstream + customer downstream
Indirect emissions from purchased electricity only
Natural emissions from forests

questions.explanation: GHG Protocol scopes — Scope 1: direct emissions (own boilers, vehicles, factories). Scope 2: indirect from purchased energy (electricity, heat, cooling). Scope 3: ALL OTHER indirect — purchased goods, business travel, employee commuting, USE of sold products, waste, distribution, investments. Scope 3 is often largest (~70-90% of corporate footprint) but hardest to measure. SEBI now mandates ESG disclosures for top-1000 listed Indian companies (BRSR — Business Responsibility & Sustainability Reporting from FY 2022-23).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The current concentration of methane (CH₄) in the atmosphere — over 2.5× pre-industrial — is approximately:

options.option_text: 200 ppb
1,920 ppb (~1.92 ppm) in 2024 (vs 720 ppb pre-industrial)
10 ppb

questions.explanation: CH₄ — second largest GHG contributor (~16-20% of warming). Sources: livestock (enteric fermentation), rice paddies, oil/gas leaks, landfills, wetlands, permafrost thaw. Atmospheric lifetime ~12 years (vs CO₂'s centuries) BUT 80× CO₂'s GWP over 20 years. Global Methane Pledge (COP-26 Glasgow 2021) aims 30% cut by 2030 — India NOT a signatory (livestock + paddy concerns). India's CH₄ emissions ~14% of global (mostly enteric fermentation from cattle).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The largest ice mass on Earth, currently losing >150 Gt/year of ice, is:

options.option_text: Greenland Ice Sheet
Antarctic Ice Sheet (~91% of global land ice; if fully melted, sea level would rise ~58 m)
Himalayan glaciers
Andes glaciers

questions.explanation: Antarctic Ice Sheet — ~26.5 million km³ ice (~91% of global ice; sea-level equivalent ~58 m if all melted). Greenland — ~2.85 million km³ (sea-level equivalent ~7.4 m). Together they hold ~99% of global freshwater ice. Currently losing — Antarctic ~150 Gt/yr (mostly West Antarctica + Antarctic Peninsula); Greenland ~270 Gt/yr accelerating. Himalayan glaciers — much smaller in volume but critical for Asian rivers (Ganga, Indus, Brahmaputra source); 'Third Pole'. ISRO's BHUVAN platform tracks Indian glaciers.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 'Keeling Curve', one of the most iconic datasets in climate science, has been tracking atmospheric concentrations at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, since 1958. Which gas does it measure?

options.option_text: Methane (CH₄), rising from ~700 ppb in pre-industrial times
Carbon dioxide (CO₂), the primary long-lived greenhouse gas
Nitrous oxide (N₂O), the third most abundant greenhouse gas
Ozone (O₃), whose tropospheric rise began in the industrial era

questions.explanation: Charles David Keeling began continuous CO₂ measurements at Mauna Loa in 1958; the resulting record, now exceeding 420 ppm, is called the Keeling Curve. Methane (Option A) is also tracked but the iconic Mauna Loa curve specifically refers to CO₂, which Keeling chose for its dominant role in the planetary radiative energy budget.

questions.stem: The Arctic is warming 2–4 times faster than the global average, a phenomenon termed 'Arctic amplification'. Which physical feedback is identified as the PRIMARY driver of this acceleration?

options.option_text: Polar vortex weakening, redirecting warm mid-latitude air masses into the Arctic
Ice-albedo feedback: melting ice exposes dark ocean, absorbing more solar energy
Permafrost methane flux accelerating local radiative forcing above the global rate
Thermohaline circulation intensification transporting tropical heat to polar regions

questions.explanation: Arctic amplification is primarily driven by the ice-albedo feedback: white sea ice (albedo ~0.8) reflects most incoming sunlight, but as it melts, the exposed dark ocean surface (albedo ~0.06) absorbs far more solar radiation, accelerating local warming. Permafrost methane release (Option C) contributes but is secondary to the albedo effect in current IPCC attribution studies.

questions.stem: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is now at its weakest in over 1,000 years according to proxy reconstructions. Which consequence would a major AMOC slowdown most directly produce?

options.option_text: Accelerated warming of the entire North Atlantic basin and the Arctic region
Significant cooling of Northwestern Europe and disruption of South Asian monsoon patterns
Intensified hurricane activity across the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean regions
Uniform global sea-level rise distributed equally across all major ocean basins

questions.explanation: AMOC acts as a heat pump, transporting warm tropical surface water to the North Atlantic and returning cold deep water southward. Its weakening reduces heat supply to Northwestern Europe — paradoxically cooling it even as global temperatures rise. Studies also link AMOC slowdown to a southward ITCZ shift that weakens South Asian monsoons. Option A is the direct opposite of the correct effect.

questions.stem: The IPCC uses 100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP₁₀₀) to compare greenhouse gases against CO₂ as the baseline. Which of the following gases carries the HIGHEST GWP₁₀₀ per IPCC AR5 values?

options.option_text: Methane (CH₄) with a GWP₁₀₀ of approximately 28–34 times CO₂
Nitrous oxide (N₂O) with a GWP₁₀₀ of approximately 265–298 times CO₂
Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆) with a GWP₁₀₀ of approximately 23,500 times CO₂
HFC-134a (common refrigerant) with a GWP₁₀₀ of approximately 1,430 times CO₂

questions.explanation: SF₆, used in high-voltage electrical switchgear, has a GWP₁₀₀ of ~23,500 (IPCC AR5) and an atmospheric lifetime exceeding 3,000 years — the highest of all regulated greenhouse gases under the Kyoto Protocol. N₂O (Option B, ~270× CO₂) is frequently confused as the highest because it is the third-largest contributor to radiative forcing, but its GWP is far below SF₆.

questions.stem: Climate scientists identify a wet-bulb temperature (TW) of 35°C as the absolute human survivability threshold even for a resting, healthy adult in shade. Why is TW = 35°C the critical limit?

options.option_text: Solar radiation at this point overwhelms the body's maximum heat absorption capacity
Sweat evaporation fails as wet-bulb equals the skin's thermodynamic heat-loss limit
Core temperature rises above 42°C irreversibly due to direct air conduction alone
Dehydration depletes plasma volume beyond the cardiovascular system's safe reserve

questions.explanation: Wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature achievable by evaporative cooling in a given environment. At TW = 35°C, the surroundings are thermodynamically as 'cool' as sweat can make the skin, so no further heat can be shed; core temperature rises fatally. Option C describes the eventual outcome of TW > 35°C, not the defining thermodynamic reason the 35°C threshold exists.

questions.stem: Aerosols exert an effective radiative forcing (ERF) of approximately −1.0 to −1.5 W m⁻² — the largest source of uncertainty in climate projections. This negative ERF arises primarily because aerosols?

options.option_text: Absorb outgoing longwave radiation and re-radiate it downward toward the surface
Reflect incoming solar radiation and brighten clouds via indirect cloud nucleation effects
Chemically react with CO₂ in the stratosphere, diminishing its radiative efficiency
Absorb stratospheric UV radiation, thereby indirectly cooling the lower troposphere

questions.explanation: Aerosols produce negative ERF (net cooling) through two pathways: (1) direct scattering of incoming shortwave solar radiation back to space, and (2) the indirect Twomey effect — aerosols serve as cloud condensation nuclei, creating more numerous but smaller cloud droplets that reflect more sunlight than natural clouds. Option A describes the longwave trapping mechanism of greenhouse gases, which aerosols do not drive.

questions.stem: 'Sea-level fingerprinting' theory predicts that rapid mass loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet would cause regions geographically CLOSEST to Greenland (e.g., Iceland, UK) to experience which counter-intuitive effect?

options.option_text: The steepest sea-level rise from meltwater runoff and amplified gravitational pull
A relative sea-level FALL due to reduced gravitational attraction and crustal rebound
No net sea-level change since meltwater redistributes evenly across all ocean basins
Enhanced rise above global mean from thermal expansion of inflowing cold meltwater

questions.explanation: Large ice sheets gravitationally attract nearby ocean water, raising regional sea levels above the global mean. As Greenland loses mass, its gravitational pull weakens, causing the locally elevated ocean water to migrate away toward lower latitudes — paradoxically lowering sea level near Greenland while distant tropical coastlines experience above-average rise. Option A reflects the most common misconception and is the opposite of what fingerprinting models predict.
